questions.question: A chart describes a patient as having cardiomegaly. The word is built from cardi/o, meaning heart, and -megaly, meaning enlargement. What does the chart say about this patient?
questions.explanation: Cardi/o (heart) + -megaly (enlargement) = an enlarged heart. The parts of the word give the meaning.

questions.question: A 65-year-old with breathing problems is under the care of a pulmonologist. The name combines pulmon/o, meaning lung, with -logist, meaning a specialist. Which patients does this doctor treat?
choices: Patients with lung and breathing disorders
questions.explanation: Pulmon/o (lung) + -logist (specialist) = a lung specialist.

questions.question: A patient's history lists arteriosclerosis. The word is built from arterio (artery), scler (hard), and -osis (condition). What is happening in this patient's body?
choices: His red blood cells are low
questions.explanation: Arterio (artery) + scler (hard) + -osis (condition) = a hardening of the arteries.

questions.question: A lab report shows a low erythrocyte count. Erythr/o means red and -cyte means cell. What is low in this patient?
questions.explanation: Erythr/o (red) + -cyte (cell) = red blood cells, so a low count means too few of them.

questions.question: Paperwork for a transfer includes a report from the patient's nephrologist. Nephr/o means kidney. That report is about the patient's:
questions.explanation: Nephr/o (kidney) + -logist (specialist) = a kidney specialist, so the report covers the kidneys.

questions.question: A patient rates his pain as 8 out of 10. Which root word means pain?
questions.explanation: Alges is the root for pain. Angi refers to vessels, asthen to weakness, and centesis to a puncture.

questions.question: A monitor shows a heart rhythm that starts above the ventricles and runs at 150 beats/min. Using supra- (above), tachy- (fast), and cardi (heart), the name of this rhythm is:
questions.explanation: Above the ventricles (supraventricular) + a fast (tachy-) heart rate (cardia) = supraventricular tachycardia.

questions.question: A pulse oximeter reads 88%, well below normal, so the patient's tissues are getting too little oxygen. The state is named with hypo-, meaning low. It is called:
questions.explanation: Hypo- (low) + oxygen = hypoxia, too little oxygen reaching the tissues.

questions.question: A crash patient's blood pressure is 90/56, lower than normal. His history shows the opposite problem, hypertension. The prefixes hypo- and hyper- tell you his current pressure is ___ and his long-standing pressure problem is ___.
questions.explanation: Hypo- means low and hyper- means high, so a low reading now is hypo- and the chronic problem, hypertension, is hyper-.

questions.question: A test records the heart's electrical activity as a printed tracing. With electro- (electrical), cardi/o (heart), and -gram (a record), that tracing is an:
questions.explanation: Electro (electrical) + cardi/o (heart) + -gram (record) = electrocardiogram, a record of the heart's electrical activity.

questions.question: A patient coughs up blood after a chest injury. The term is built from hem/o (blood) and -ptysis (spitting). It is called:
questions.explanation: Hem/o (blood) + -ptysis (spitting) = hemoptysis, coughing or spitting up blood. Vomiting blood is hematemesis.

questions.question: A test bounces sound waves (echo-) off the heart and records how the valves move. With cardi/o (heart) and -gram (a record), this test is an:
questions.explanation: Echo (sound) + cardi/o (heart) + -gram (record) = echocardiogram, a sound-wave record of the heart.

questions.question: After a motorcycle crash, a 17-year-old tells you he sees two of everything. The term is built from dipl- (double) and -opia (vision condition). He has:
questions.explanation: Dipl- (double) + -opia (vision) = diplopia, double vision.

questions.question: Both of a patient's hands show the same blue discoloration, cyanosis (cyan = blue, -osis = condition). Because it appears on both sides, you document it as:
questions.explanation: Both hands means both sides, and bi- means two — bilateral. Cyan is blue, so the condition is cyanosis.

questions.question: A paramedic starts an IV in the patient's left antecubital area. Ante- means front or before, and cubit refers to the elbow. The line went into a vein at the:
questions.explanation: Ante- (front) + cubit (elbow) = the front of the elbow, the usual IV site there.

questions.question: You arrive at a crash and find a 17-year-old lying face down on the pavement. For your report, the position you found him in is documented as:
questions.explanation: Face down is the prone position. Supine is face up.

questions.question: A patient reports weakness on his left side only, and the right side tests normal. Uni- means one. You document the weakness as:
questions.explanation: One side only is unilateral (uni- = one). Bilateral would mean both sides.

questions.question: A PCR lists the abbreviation ASHD in a patient's history. Built from arteriosclerosis (hardened arteries) and heart disease, ASHD stands for:
questions.explanation: ASHD = arteriosclerotic heart disease, heart disease caused by hardened arteries.

questions.question: Before listing today's problems, a PCR has a PMH section where the crew writes the patient's 2019 heart attack and his diabetes. PMH covers the patient's:
questions.explanation: PMH = past medical history — conditions and events from before this call.

questions.question: A patient tells you he has no allergies to any medications or foods. The accepted abbreviation for the allergy field of your report is:
questions.explanation: NKA = no known allergies, the standard abbreviation for the allergy field.

questions.question: On a transfer, two agencies use the same abbreviation to mean different things, and the receiving crew misreads when a treatment was given. This call shows the main danger of abbreviations: they
choices: Are banned on patient care reports
Cannot be typed into documentation software
Can mean different things in different contexts
Are written in all capital letters
questions.explanation: The same abbreviation can carry different meanings for different agencies or contexts, which is how misreadings happen.
